newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG mercenary tale straight from pages of thriller.
newsitem.headline: PNG mercenary tale straight from pages of thriller.

text.p: For the past two weeks a courtroom in Papua New Guinea has heard a tale of clandestine meetings around the world, African mercenaries and multimillion dollar international financial transfers.

The official inquiry into a US$36 million mercenary deal which last month sparked an army revolt, forcing then prime minister Sir Julius Chan to step aside, could have come straight from the pages of a Frederick Forsyth thriller.

But the final chapter has yet to unfold since most of the evidence so far has come only from mercenary leader Tim Spicer and sacked army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, who staged the rebellion.
Chan, his deputy prime minister Chris Haiveta and defence minister Matias Ijape, who were also forced to stepped aside, have still to appear before the inquiry commission.
According to Singirok, the mercenary tale began in 1996.

Frustrated at being unable to end a nine-year secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island, which has haemorrhaged millions of dollars since rebels forced the closure of a giant copper mine, the PNG government sought outside military help.

Negotiations began in early 1996 with the German firm International Business Company on a US$24 million contract for troop training between December 1996 and July 1997 and weapons that included M17 and M18 helicopters.

But Singirok, who conducted the negotiations, said the government pressured him to drop the German deal and talk to British-based military consultancy Sandline International about African mercenaries.
Singirok said then defence minister Ijape told him: "Bro (brother), you can become a rich man if you engage this group."
HATCHED IN COFFEE SHOP
The mercenary deal, codenamed "Oyster", was formally hatched during a three-hour meeting on April 7, 1996 in the coffee shop at the Hilton Hotel in the Australian resort town of Cairns.

The cafe, normally full of newly-wed Japanese, was the venue that Easter Sunday of a rendezvous between Spicer, a Scots Guard turned mercenary, Singirok, Ijape and international mining entrepreneur Tony Buckingham.
Spicer, Sandline's chief executive, told the inquiry the PNG group wanted military support on Bougainville, including two Russian-built MI-24 attack helicopters.

A month later he handed a written proposal to Singirok, a wounded veteran of the Bougainville conflict, when the PNG commander visited Sandline's smart offices on King's Road in London's fashionable Chelsea district.
Singirok said British arms dealer Franklins paid his London hotel bill and flew him to Belfast to inspect armaments.
He said there was another London meeting in September between Spicer, PNG's then deputy prime minister Haiveta, and Rupert McCowan from Hong Kong finance house Jardine Fleming.
Singirok told the inquiry McCowan acted as financial adviser in the mercenary deal.
A Jardine Fleming spokesman in Hong Kong said McCowan had been suspended indefinitely and an internal inquiry had been launched after its involvement surfaced at the PNG inquiry.
Jardine Fleming was one of the lead managers in November's float of Orogen, which has a stake in some major PNG gold and petroleum projects and is 51-percent owned by the government.
Two weeks after its float, Orogen's shares surged. Orogen has since said it was not involved in the mercenary deal.
DEAL IS SIGNED
Further secret meetings occurred in late 1996 in Port Moresby, Cairns and in Hong Kong, and the contract was finally signed on January 31 in the PNG capital.

Present at the signing in the offices of the PNG Banking Corp, a government-owned commercial bank, were Spicer, McCowan and a PNG finance official, but not Chan, Haiveta or Ijape. Singirok said he then privately opposed the deal and was "out fishing" that day.
On signing the deal, the PNG government transferred US$18 million to the Hong Kong account of Sandline.
When news of the mercenary deal broke in The Australian newspaper a month later, Chan said the mercenaries were merely advisers who would train troops but not fight rebels.

Yet, the 10-page contract committed Sandline to deploying 70-odd mercenaries for offensive operations on Bougainville with the aim of recapturing the giant Panguna copper mine and buying an arsenal of weapons for PNG, including four Russian-built helicopters, rocket launchers and night vision equipment.
The weapons are now on an Australian airforce base awaiting a decision by the PNG government on whether to let them into the country, given the uncertainty of the army's loyalty.
MINERS AND MERCENARIES
Africa's best known private army, Executive Outcomes, which provided Sandline with the mercenaries, was reported to have been partly paid for its work through mining concessions.

Both Spicer and Chan denied the PNG deal included any mining concessions for Sandline or any associated firm, despite a letter signed by Spicer suggesting a Panguna joint-venture between Sandline, PNG and Anglo-Australian miner RTZ-CRA.
In February 1997, before the mercenary deal became public, sizable blocks of shares in RTZ-CRA's Bougainville Copper Ltd, which runs the Panguna mine, were bought in Australia.
On March 2, Chan announced a government plan to buy out the 53 percent stake in BCL held by RTZ-CRA, but gave no details.
Jardine Fleming said it was asked by the PNG government to advise on the buy-out, but no formal contract was received.

On March 17, Singirok demanded on national radio that Chan resign within 48 hours over the mercenary deal, labelling it corrupt. Chan sacked Singirok, sparking an army revolt and two days of violence and looting in Port Moresby.

Spicer's mercenaries were thrown out of the country, but the 20-year British army veteran, honoured by Britain's Queen Elizabeth for his services in Northern Ireland, was detained by rebel troops. Spicer told the inquiry rebel troops held a gun to his head and threatened him with death several times.

Spicer, 44, was eventually released into police custody after being arrested on illegal firearm charges. In his first court appearance, he carried a biography of Ian Fleming, creator of 007 James Bond, and pleaded not guilty.
He staunchly defended his company, telling journalists not to call his men mercenaries, but consultants. "There is nothing wrong with the activities of Sandline," he said.
The charges against Spicer were dropped after he concluded his evidence at the inquiry, allowing him to return to London.
Chan, Haiveta and Ijape stepped aside on March 26 pending the mercenary inquiry, which has been extended until May 30 so they can give evidence.
